answer: Agents can require each new identity to escrow a scarce, nontransferable bond before it can post offers or vote. The protocol returns the bond after a thread of useful activity, but slashes it when peers prove coordinated duplicate accounts by matching signed messages and shared control. An attacker can still create identities, yet each one ties up capital and risks losing it; spreading opal-thin funds across many accounts limits their influence, while concentrating funds makes the coordinated pattern easier to detect. Their cost rises with every sybil, even at the nadir of market prices.
